text: Nine lessons ago, this project started with a worried sentence from Dale Granger over coffee: can you tighten things up, and let me actually know if something gets through. Here's everything that sentence turned into.

A specific scope: four named servers, a documented baseline, one detection target tied to the near-miss. A real standard, CIS Level 1, scoped down to exactly what applies. The Windows checklist applied and verified on two servers. The Linux checklist applied and verified on the other two.

A real, sequence-aware KQL rule against SigninLogs. Tested against three synthetic scenarios before ever being trusted. Documented in a runbook and a changelog, so none of it depends on one person's memory. Presented to Dale with a live demonstration. And a real pushback question, answered with evidence, not reassurance.

None of these lessons were really about CIS Benchmarks or KQL alone -- each one used those tools to practice a transferable skill. Requirements clarification, verified hardening, testing a detection before trusting it, making knowledge reusable, and communicating technical risk clearly. A hiring manager cares about that list far more than which exact command got typed.

This project was scoped smaller than Hartwell's full security program on purpose -- four servers, Level 1, one rule, one stakeholder's sign-off. That wasn't a limitation to apologize for. It was the correct scope for what Dale actually asked for.

One hardened handful of servers and one detection rule is a real start, not a finish line. Hartwell's security program will need to grow well beyond this project -- more systems, a broader library of detection rules, and a level of process no single analyst can carry alone. What that growth looks like is its own body of work, picked up elsewhere.
